  [Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd).
:::

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and *left* and *right*
are always the offense's. Q is the quarterback, R the running back, Y and U the tight ends, and X, Z
and H the wide receivers; C is the center. On defense, E and T are the ends and tackles, S, M and W the
Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, $ the nickel back, CB the cornerbacks and FS and SS the safeties. Lines
ending in a bar are blocks, arrows are paths, and a dashed brown arrow is the throw. The yellow line is
the line to gain. In the charts, ["neutral situations"](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-neutral-situation) means what it meant in
[01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd): outside the last two minutes of
each half, with each team's win probability between 20% and 80%, so that the score and the clock
aren't making the call.

## The situation comes before the play

A play-caller does not walk into a game with a list of "good plays" and pick his favorite. He walks in
with a [call sheet](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-call-sheet), the laminated card you see covering
his mouth on the sideline, and that card is organized by **situation**. One box for first-and-10, one for
second-and-long, one for second-and-short, a few for third down cut by distance, then boxes for the
places on the field where the rules of the game change the math: backed up against your own goal line,
coming out, the red zone, the goal line. A separate panel handles the clock: the
[two-minute drill](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd) and the
[four-minute offense](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd), where the
score and the time left are the situation.

Strip away the score and the clock and three numbers define a situation: the down, the distance to the
line to gain, and the yard line. This chapter is about all three on the first two downs of a series,
and about the yard line everywhere.

Start with the downs. First and second down are the
[**early downs**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-early-down): the snaps where the offense still has
at least one more try in hand before the down that decides whether it punts. That one extra try is
what makes them different. On third down the offense *must* gain the yards, and the defense knows it,
so third down gets its own chapter ([Third Down: The Money Down](10-02-third-down.qmd)). On an early down
nothing is forced. A play-caller can run, throw short, throw deep, fake one and do the other, and the
defense has to be ready for all of it. Early downs are also most of the game: about three snaps in four
are first or second downs.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game you see the same playbook menu on every snap, and the "situation" is something you
notice if you feel like it. A real play-caller's options are *pre-filtered* by situation before the
game starts. On his own 2-yard line, half of his passing game is crossed off the sheet; on
second-and-1 a box of deep shots appears that he would never call on second-and-11. When you hear a
coordinator say "we were in a good situation for that call," he means the call was on the right part
of the sheet.
:::

## First down: the freest snap in football

If any snap is a true guess for the defense, it's first-and-10. Here is how often offenses have
thrown on it, in neutral situations, for every season the play-by-play covers:

```{python}
#| label: fig-first-down-trend
#| fig-cap: "Left: how often offenses passed on first-and-10 (blue) and on second down (orange), neutral situations, every regular season from 1999 to 2025. A pass is a called pass, so sacks and scrambles count. First-and-10 has barely moved in 27 years; second down has drifted toward the pass. Right: what each choice earned on first-and-10, in EPA per play. A dropback beat a run in every one of the 27 seasons, by roughly 0.15 to 0.25 points a play. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.9), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.32))
yrs = TREND.index.values
a1.plot(yrs, TREND.values * 100, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, label="1st & 10")
a1.plot(yrs, TREND2.values * 100, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, label="2nd down (any distance)")
a1.set_ylim(35, 70)
a1.set_ylabel("Pass rate (%)", fontsize=8)
a1.axhline(50, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
a1.text(2009.5, 50.4, "coin flip", fontsize=6.5, color=style.MUTED, va="bottom", ha="center")
a1.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7, handlelength=1.5)
a1.set_title("How often they pass", fontsize=9)
a2.plot(yrs, GAP[1].values, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, label="dropbacks")
a2.plot(yrs, GAP[0].values, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, label="designed runs")
a2.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
a2.set_ylabel("EPA per play, 1st & 10", fontsize=8)
a2.set_ylim(-0.2, 0.2)
a2.legend(loc="center right", fontsize=7, handlelength=1.5, bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.62))
a2.set_title("What each one earned", fontsize=9)
for a in (a1, a2):
    a.set_xticks([2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025])
    a.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

Two facts sit side by side in that chart, and the tension between them is the whole early-down debate.

The first fact: **first-and-10 is a coin flip, and it always has been.** In every season since 1999,
offenses in neutral situations have thrown on between `{python} pct(S["f10_lo"])` and
`{python} pct(S["f10_hi"])` of their first-and-10 snaps (`{python} pct(S["f10_25"])` in 2025). Over
the same years the league remade itself: the shotgun went from a passing-down formation to the
default, the spread arrived from college, the rules protected quarterbacks and receivers more every
few years. Second down moved with it, from about `{python} pct(S["p2_99"])` passes in the first five seasons of
the data to about `{python} pct(S["p2_25"])` in the last five. First down didn't.[^trend]

The second fact: **the pass has been the better bet on first-and-10 every single year.** A dropback out-earned
a designed run by between `{python} f'{S["gap_lo"]:.2f}'` and `{python} f'{S["gap_hi"]:.2f}'` points
of EPA per play, and the run has averaged a *loss* of expected points in all 27 seasons. A tenth of a
point per play, you'll remember from [01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd),
is roughly the gap between a good offense and an average one. So the obvious question: if passing on
first down is that much better, why hasn't anyone's first-down pass rate moved?

There are four honest answers, and none of them is "coaches are fools."

1. **The averages aren't a fair fight.** First-down runs and passes are not run against the same
   defenses. Offenses call passes when the defense looks ready for the run, and many first-down passes
   are play-action, which borrows its value from the run's existence. Take the run away and the pass
   faces a defense that knows it's coming. ([Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd)
   calls this a selection effect and walks through it.)
2. **Balance is the point of first down.** First-and-10 is the one snap where the defense can't lean.
   A team that throws 80% of the time on first down has handed the defense a
   [tendency](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency), and the defense will play pass on first down
   until the edge is gone. In the language of [08-02](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd),
   the run is what keeps the pass from being a guess the defense wins.
3. **Coaches price risk, not just averages.** A run almost never loses ten yards or the ball; a pass
   sometimes does both. EPA counts sacks and interceptions in its average, but a head coach who answers
   for every turnover on Monday weighs a disaster more heavily than a bonus. The economist David Romer
   found the same lean in NFL fourth-down decisions twenty years ago.[^romer]
4. **Runs buy things EPA doesn't price.** A run keeps the clock moving when you're ahead, keeps a pass
   rush from teeing off on every snap, and spares your quarterback a hit.

Weigh those and you get the position most analysts actually hold. It isn't "never run." It's that the
*average* first-down run has been a worse bet than the average first-down pass for a generation, that
most teams could throw a little more on early downs before the pass's edge wore off, and that the
teams who do it well tend to have the better offenses. That "how much more than expected" idea has a
name, [pass rate over expected (PROE)](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-proe), and a chapter of its own
([Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)).

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: balance on first down"}
First-and-10 is balanced because balance is what first down is *for*. It is the one snap where
a defense has nothing to go on but the formation and the film, so a play-caller who keeps it near a coin
flip forces the defense to defend everything, and makes every later down easier to call. The price is
the gap in the chart: each first-down run called "to stay balanced" gives up, on average, a slice of
expected points. The good offenses keep the balance and shrink the price, with runs that look exactly
like their passes and passes that look exactly like their runs.
:::

### On schedule and behind schedule

Coaches don't talk about first down in EPA. They talk about the *schedule*. An offense is
[**on schedule**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-on-schedule-behind-schedule) when its early downs
leave it a manageable next down: about 4 yards or more on first-and-10, then about half of what's left
on second down, so that third down is short or never comes. It's **behind schedule** when a short gain,
a loss, a sack, an incompletion or a penalty leaves second-and-long or third-and-long. The yardage
version of success rate you met in [13-02](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd),
40% of the yards on first down and 60% on second, is the schedule turned into a number.

Why 4 yards? Because of what each first-down result does to the *rest* of the series:

```{python}
#| label: fig-on-schedule
#| fig-cap: "What a first-and-10 play sets up: the chance the series ends in a first down or a touchdown, by the yards the first-down play gained (neutral situations between the offense's own 20 and the opponent's 30, 2016-2025 regular seasons; plays that ended in a turnover are left out). A 0 includes incompletions; 'loss' includes sacks. Each bar is labelled with the second down it leaves. Every yard helps, by three or four percentage points of conversion; the costliest result is a loss. Coaches draw the 'on schedule' line at about 4 yards, where second down is 6 or shorter. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
xs = list(SCHED.index)
labs = ["loss"] + [str(g) for g in range(0, 10)] + ["10+"]
cols = [style.DEFENSE if g < 4 else style.OFFENSE for g in xs]
cols[-1] = style.THIRD
ax.bar(range(len(xs)), SCHED.succ.values * 100, color=cols, width=0.72, zorder=3)
for i, (g, v) in enumerate(zip(xs, SCHED.succ.values)):
    ax.text(i, v * 100 + 1.5, f"{v * 100:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK)
    nxt = "2nd &\n11+" if g < 0 else ("1st\ndown" if g >= 10 else f"2nd &\n{10 - g}")
    ax.text(i, 4, nxt, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=5.6, color="white", linespacing=1.0, zorder=4,
            fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(xs)), labs, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Yards gained on first-and-10", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Series converted (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 112)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.text(1.6, 104, "behind schedule", ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(7.5, 104, "on schedule", ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontweight="bold")
ax.axvline(4.5, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), ymax=0.9)
plt.show()
```

Read the bars as the price of first down. A first-down play that loses yards (a sack, a run stuffed
in the backfield) leaves a series that converts only `{python} pct(S["sched_loss"])` of the time; an
incompletion or a no-gain run, `{python} pct(S["sched_0"])`. After that there's no cliff: every yard is
worth three or four points of conversion, and 4 yards gets the series to `{python} pct(S["sched_4"])`.
Coaches draw the line at about 4 because second-and-6 or shorter still leaves room for a run *and* a
pass, and puts a third-and-short within one ordinary play. The EPA bookkeeping from
[01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) lands in nearly the same place:
the smallest first-and-10 gain whose average EPA is positive is `{python} S["be_1_10"]` yards. The
coaches' rule of thumb and the analysts' model describe the same slope and draw the line within a yard
of each other.

The bars also show what coaches fear most on first down, and it isn't the incompletion. It's the
**negative play**. A sack or a tackle for loss (`{python} pct(S["share_loss"])` of these first downs)
does more damage than an incompletion, because it spends the down *and* lengthens the distance. A
holding penalty is worse still: first-and-20. That is why so much of the modern early-down passing
game is built to be safe as well as productive (the quick game, screens, play-action with the
quarterback rolling away from pressure) and why a quarterback who takes a sack on first down hears
about it in the film room.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Second-and-long is no big deal: you still have two downs." Look at the bars again. A first-down play
that gains nothing leaves a series that converts `{python} pct(S["sched_0"])` of the time; a 4-yard gain
leaves one that converts `{python} pct(S["sched_4"])`. Two downs to gain ten yards is a much harder problem than three downs,
and the defense knows it: on second-and-long it can start playing the pass.
:::

### "Establish the run": what the claim says, and what survives

Every broadcast has an announcer who says a team needs to "establish the run": run the ball early and
often, and good things will follow. It is one of the oldest pieces of football wisdom, and it is really
four different claims bundled together. The data treats them very differently.

**Claim 1: running wears the defense down, so the runs get better as the game goes on.** If that were
true, early-down runs in close games should gain more in the fourth quarter than in the first. They
barely do. From 2016 to 2025 they averaged `{python} signed(QRUN.loc[1])` EPA in the first quarter and
`{python} signed(QRUN.loc[4])` in the fourth, a hair better and nowhere near closing the gap to passes,
which averaged `{python} signed(QPASS.loc[1])` and `{python} signed(QPASS.loc[4])`.[^quarters] Big,
physical offenses do tire defenses on some days, and you'll see it on individual drives. It just
doesn't show up as a rule.

**Claim 2: you have to run to make play-action work.** This one has been tested hardest, and it
fails. [Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
walks through the evidence: play-action passes beat ordinary dropbacks by about the same margin
whether a team's run game is good, bad or barely used. Linebackers react to the *look* of the run
(the line's first step, the back's path) because reacting is their job, not because a running back
has been gaining yards. What survives is the weaker point: the fake has to look exactly like your
real run, so you need a real run to copy.

**Claim 3: teams that run the ball win.** This is the claim that keeps the phrase alive, because the
correlation is real and enormous. Here it is, beside the version of it that matters:

```{python}
#| label: fig-establish-run
#| fig-cap: "Two ways to connect running and winning, every regular-season team-game from 2016 to 2025 (ties left out). Left: win rate by how many designed runs a team called in the game. Teams with 31 or more runs won more than four times in five. Right: win rate by how often the team ran on first and second down in the first half, split into five equal-sized groups. The line is flat: running a lot early told you nothing about who would win. The difference is direction. Teams run a lot because they are ahead (protecting a lead, running out the clock), not ahead because they ran. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.9), sharey=True, gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.12))
for a, tab, title, xl in [(a1, WIN_RUNS, "By total runs in the game", "Designed runs called"),
                          (a2, WIN_H1, "By first-half early-down run rate", "Run rate on 1st and 2nd down, 1st half")]:
    xs_ = range(len(tab))
    a.bar(xs_, tab["mean"] * 100, color=style.SERIES[0] if a is a1 else style.MUTED, width=0.68, zorder=3)
    for i, v in zip(xs_, tab["mean"]):
        a.text(i, v * 100 + 1.5, f"{v * 100:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=style.INK)
    a.set_xticks(list(xs_), [str(i) for i in tab.index], fontsize=6.6)
    a.set_xlabel(xl, fontsize=7.5)
    a.set_title(title, fontsize=8.6)
    a.axhline(50, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
a1.set_ylabel("Won the game (%)", fontsize=8)
a1.set_ylim(0, 100)
plt.show()
```

On the left, the famous version: teams that ran more than 30 times won `{python} pct(S["w30"])` of
their games; teams that ran 20 times or fewer won `{python} pct(S["w20"])`. On the right, the version a
play-caller can actually choose: how much a team leaned on the run on early downs in the *first half*,
before the score had a say. Every fifth of that scale won about half its games.[^establish]

The left panel runs backward. A team that leads in the fourth quarter runs to drain the clock (the
[four-minute offense](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)), and a team
that trails throws to catch up. Across these games, a team's fourth-quarter run rate correlated with
winning at `{python} f'{S["c_q4"]:.2f}'`; its first-half early-down run rate, at
`{python} f'{S["c_h1"]:.2f}'`. Winning causes running. Running, by itself, doesn't cause winning.

**Claim 4: the run keeps the defense honest.** This one survives, and it's the reason the debate never
ends. A defense that doesn't have to respect the run can drop seven or eight players into coverage on
every early down, rush four, and make the pass much harder. The run's value isn't only its own EPA;
part of it shows up in the pass's EPA. That is constraint theory again, and it explains why the best
offenses of the analytics era did not simply stop running. It also explains what *does* make a run
game worth leaning on: being **efficient**, not being frequent. A run that gains as much as a pass
(because the defense is outnumbered, or because the quarterback is a running threat) is worth calling
often. A run that's merely "establishing" something is the price you pay for balance.

```{python}
#| label: fig-team-early-downs
#| fig-cap: "Every offense from 2016 to 2025 (320 team-seasons) on first and second down in neutral situations: how often it passed (across) and what it earned per play (up). The dashed lines are the averages. The cloud tilts up a little, since passing more goes with scoring more, but loosely: the best offenses of the decade sit on both sides of the average pass rate. The five labelled seasons are this chapter's case studies. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.9))
ax.scatter(TEAM.pr * 100, TEAM.epa, s=14, color=style.MUTED, alpha=0.45, edgecolor="none", zorder=2)
ax.axvline(TEAM.pr.mean() * 100, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(TEAM.epa.mean(), color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
OFFS = {(2018, "KC"): (8, 6, "left"), (2018, "LA"): (8, 10, "left"), (2019, "BAL"): (0, 14, "center"),
        (2023, "DET"): (-8, -14, "right"), (2024, "DET"): (10, 12, "left")}
for k, name in CASES.items():
    t = TEAM.loc[k]
    col = style.SERIES[1] if k[1] == "BAL" else (style.SERIES[2] if k[1] == "DET" else style.SERIES[0])
    ax.scatter([t.pr * 100], [t.epa], s=46, color=col, edgecolor="white", lw=0.8, zorder=4)
    dx, dy, ha = OFFS[k]
    ax.annotate(name, (t.pr * 100, t.epa), xytext=(dx, dy), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=7.5,
                color=style.INK, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=5,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=4))
ax.set_xlabel("Pass rate on first and second down (%)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per play, first and second down", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.text(TEAM.pr.mean() * 100 + 0.3, ax.get_ylim()[0] + 0.01, "league average", fontsize=6.5, color=style.MUTED,
        va="bottom")
plt.show()
```

The chart is the debate in one picture. Passing more goes with better offense, but loosely (a
correlation of `{python} f'{S["c_team"]:.2f}'` across these team-seasons): plenty of pass-happy teams
were bad, and some of the best offenses of the decade ran more than average. What every season in the
top band shares is efficiency on *both* kinds of play, or a run game good enough that the usual price
of running wasn't there. The three film-room boxes take the labelled seasons one at a time.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs and Los Angeles Rams, 2018"}
**The season:** a year the analytics argument still points to, because the two best offenses in
football leaned on early-down passing. Kansas City (12–4) led the NFL with 565 points in Patrick
Mahomes's first season as a starter; the Rams (13–3), in Sean McVay's second season, were second with
527.[^kcla] In neutral situations on first and second down, the Chiefs ranked
`{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2018, "KC"), "pr_rk"])` in how often they passed and first in EPA per play;
the Rams ranked only `{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2018, "LA"), "pr_rk"])` in how often they passed but
`{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2018, "LA"), "epa_rk"])` in what they earned, with a play-action game built to look
exactly like their outside-zone runs (the [Rams film room in 04-05](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
has the details).

**The game:** Monday night, November 19, 2018, moved from Mexico City to the Los Angeles Memorial
Coliseum six days before kickoff because of the condition of the field in Mexico. The Rams won 54–51. Mahomes
threw for 478 yards and six touchdowns, with three interceptions; Jared Goff threw for 413 and four
touchdowns, and the two defenses scored three touchdowns between them on turnovers.[^game54] Both
offenses threw on about seven of every ten first downs that night.

**What to notice:** the Rams' passing rate is the lesson. "Pass more on early downs" was never the whole
recipe. The Rams were only a little above average in how often they threw; what set them apart was how
much each early-down pass earned, and that their runs (`{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2018, "LA"), "run_epa_rk"])`
in early-down run EPA) were good enough that the defense had to honor them on every snap. Kansas City's
runs ranked `{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2018, "KC"), "run_epa_rk"])`. The best early-down offenses of 2018 were
efficient at both, and leaned toward the pass.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Baltimore Ravens, 2019"}
**The season:** the counter-example every "pass more" chart has to answer. The 2019 Ravens went 14–2,
led the NFL with 531 points and ran for 3,296 yards, the most by any team in NFL history, with Lamar
Jackson setting the quarterback record of 1,206 rushing yards on his way to a unanimous MVP award.[^bal19]
On first and second down in neutral situations they passed *less often than any other team*
(`{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2019, "BAL"), "pr_rk"])` of 32), and they were *first* in EPA per play.

**What to notice:** their runs were first in the league in early-down EPA too
(`{python} signed(TEAM.loc[(2019, "BAL"), "run_epa"])` per run, against a league average close to
`{python} signed(ED[ED["pass"] == 0].epa.mean())`). A quarterback who is a real running threat changes the
arithmetic of the run game: on option and quarterback-run plays the defense has to account for one more
ball carrier, so the offense effectively gains a blocker
([Option Football](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) shows how). When a run is as good as a
pass, "establishing" it costs nothing, and calling it often is simply good football. The Ravens weren't
proof that running wins; they were proof that *efficient* running wins.

**The coda:** in the divisional round, the Titans jumped ahead and beat them 28–12. Behind on the
scoreboard, the Ravens threw on about three of every four early downs that night, and the offense built
on the run's threat looked ordinary. Situation decides even for the best run game in history. (The whole Baltimore era is
[a case study of its own](../12-case-studies/12-05-ravens-lamar-run-game.qmd).)
:::

## Second down: four buckets

Second down is where the schedule shows up. Whatever happened on first down sets the distance, and the
distance sorts second downs into four buckets that call for different football:

```{python}
#| label: fig-second-down
#| fig-cap: "Second down by bucket, neutral situations, 2021-2025 regular seasons. Left: how often offenses passed. Middle: EPA per play for designed runs (orange) and dropbacks (blue). Right: how often each one gained a first down on the spot. The pass earns more in every bucket, by the least on second-and-short, where runs convert two times in three. The play-action share is the percentage of each bucket's passes that faked a handoff (FTN charting, 2022-2025). Source: nflverse play-by-play and FTN charting."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 2.5), sharey=True, gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.0, 1.2, 1.2],
                                                                                  wspace=0.10))
ys = np.arange(len(SB))[::-1]
a0, a1, a2 = axes
a0.barh(ys, SEC.pr.values * 100, color=style.SERIES[0], height=0.6, zorder=3)
for y_, v in zip(ys, SEC.pr.values):
    a0.text(v * 100 + 2, y_, f"{v * 100:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK)
a0.set_xlim(0, 112); a0.set_xticks([0, 50, 100], ["0", "50", "100%"], fontsize=6.8)
a0.set_title("Pass rate", fontsize=8.5)
a0.set_yticks(ys, [f"2nd & {b}\nplay-action {PA2.loc[b]:.0%}" for b in SB], fontsize=6.8)
for a, tab, title, fmt, lim in [(a1, SEC_EPA, "EPA per play", lambda v: signed(v), (-0.2, 0.2)),
                                (a2, SEC_FD, "First down on the play", lambda v: f"{v:.0%}", (0, 0.8))]:
    for k, (col, lab) in enumerate([(style.SERIES[1], "run"), (style.SERIES[0], "dropback")]):
        vals = tab[k].values
        a.scatter(vals, ys, s=34, color=col, zorder=3, label=lab, edgecolor="white", lw=0.6)
    for y_, r0, r1 in zip(ys, tab[0].values, tab[1].values):
        a.plot([r0, r1], [y_, y_], color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.4, zorder=2)
    a.set_xlim(*lim)
    a.set_title(title, fontsize=8.5)
    a.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=6.8)
    a.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
a1.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9)
a1.set_xticks([-0.1, 0, 0.1], [MINUS + "0.1", "0", "+0.1"])
a2.set_xticks([0.2, 0.4, 0.6], ["20%", "40%", "60%"])
a1.legend(loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, -0.36), ncol=2, fontsize=7)
for a in axes:
    a.set_ylim(-0.6, len(SB) - 0.4)
plt.show()
```

- **Second-and-long (7 to 10)** is the most common second down, the usual result of an incompletion or
  a short run. The offense is behind schedule, and its job is to get *half of it back*: a 5-yard gain
  turns third-and-long into third-and-short. Offenses throw about two times in three, and the pass is
  clearly the better bet.
- **Second-and-very-long (11 or more)** follows a sack, a penalty or a loss. Offenses throw more than
  four times in five, and defenses play deep, conceding the short throw (the second drill in
  [01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) shows that picture). The goal
  is a makeable third down, not the whole distance, which is where the
  [draw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-draw-play) and the [screen](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-screen)
  earn their place.
- **Second-and-medium (4 to 6)** is the true toss-up: offenses split almost exactly half and half,
  even though the pass has out-earned the run by a wide margin here too. An offense here is on schedule,
  and every call on the sheet is live.
- **Second-and-short (1 to 3)** is a running down in practice: offenses ran on
  `{python} pct(1 - SEC.loc[SB[0], "pr"])` of these snaps (and on `{python} pct(S["run_2_1"])` of
  second-and-1s). It is also, in theory, the best passing down in football. That contradiction gets its
  own section.

### Why second-and-short is a shot down

Every coach knows the logic, and you heard it from the analyst in the opening paragraph. On
second-and-1 the offense has two downs to gain one yard. It can afford to *spend* one of them on a
[shot play](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shot-play), a pass aimed deep down the field, because if
the shot falls incomplete it's third-and-1, the easiest third down there is. Three things make the
shot unusually good here, and the first one can be measured.

**1. Failure is cheap.** Losing a down costs less on second-and-short than anywhere else. From
second-and-1, a series converted `{python} pct(S["s2_1"])` of the time; from third-and-1,
`{python} pct(S["s3_1"])`. A wasted second down cost `{python} pts(S["cost1"])` percentage points of
conversion. From second-and-5 or longer, a wasted down cost about `{python} pts(S["cost7"])` points on
average: from second-and-10 to third-and-10 is `{python} pct(S["s2_10"])` to
`{python} pct(S["s3_10"])`. The same incompletion is about half as expensive on second-and-1.[^cost]

**2. The defense is in run mode.** Second-and-short looks like a run down because it usually is one,
so defenses answer it like one: [base](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-base-defense) personnel, an
eighth defender in the [box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box), often a safety walked down,
which leaves [one deep safety](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-high) to cover the whole middle of
the field. Linebackers on short yardage are coached to attack the line the moment they see a run
action, because a yard is all the offense needs.

**3. The offense's own look sells the run.** Teams often answer second-and-short with heavy personnel
and the quarterback under center, the same look they run from, so a run fake is believable. On
second-and-short, `{python} pct(PA2.loc[SB[0]])` of passes were play-action, against
`{python} pct(PA2.loc[SB[2]])` on second-and-long and `{python} pct(PA2.loc[SB[3]])` on
second-and-very-long.

Put those together and this is what the shot looks like:

```{python}
#| label: fig-shot
#| fig-cap: "A second-and-1 shot (illustrative; frame strip in print, video on the website). The offense shows its run look: two tight ends (Y and U), the quarterback under center, the back behind him. The defense answers with base personnel and eight men within a few yards of the ball, the strong safety (red ring) walked down on the left; only the free safety (purple ring) is deep. The quarterback fakes the handoff, and the linebackers and the strong safety step up to stop a run that isn't coming. Eight players stay in to block, and only two go out: X on a post from the left, Z on a deep over route from the right (the yankee concept from 04-04). The free safety can't cover both; when he drifts toward the post, the over is open behind the linebackers. If the throw falls incomplete, it's third-and-1."
LOS_SHOT = 55.0
def shot_play():
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                    O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"),
                    O("X", "WR", -1.5, -15.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -6.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("1", -1), "T"),
           D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 6.4, "E"),
           D("SAM", "SAM", 4.0, 6.0, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -3.2, "W"),
           D("SS", "SS", 5.5, -7.2, "SS"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 14.5, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.5, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS_SHOT, to_go=1)
    # the line fires out as if it were a run, then holds its ground: eight men protect
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "Y", "U"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.35, 0.0)], speed=1.2)
    for k, dw in (("WDE", (-0.6, 0.6)), ("WDT", (-0.6, 0.0)), ("SDT", (-0.6, 0.0)), ("SDE", (-0.6, -0.6))):
        p.rush(k, pts=[dw], speed=0.8)                           # the rushers are engaged at the line
    p.path("QB", [(-1.4, 1.0)], speed=4.0)                       # open to the back for the fake
    p.path("QB", [(-4.6, -0.8)], speed=4.2)                      # then set up deep
    p.path("RB", [(3.6, 1.4)], speed=5.5)                        # the fake: the same track as the run
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.9, 0.5)], speed=2.0)                   # then he stays in to block
    p.route("X", [(11.0, 0.0), (25.0, 11.0)], frame="field")     # post from the left, breaking inside
    p.route("Z", [(7.0, -1.0), (15.5, -9.0), (18.0, -24.0)], frame="field")   # deep over from the right
    for k, to in (("SAM", (2.6, 5.0)), ("MIKE", (2.8, 1.6)), ("WILL", (3.0, -2.0)), ("SS", (3.2, -5.6))):
        st = p.players[k]
        p.path(k, [(to[0] - st.d, to[1] - st.w)], speed=3.8)      # the run fake pulls them up
    for k, to in (("SAM", (7.5, 3.5)), ("MIKE", (8.0, -0.5)), ("WILL", (7.5, -5.0)), ("SS", (7.5, -10.0))):
        st = p._cur(k)
        p.path(k, [(to[0] - st[0], to[1] - st[1])], speed=4.0)    # ...then turn to chase, too late
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, -1.0), speed=3.0)
    p.drop("FS", (21.5, -3.5), speed=4.2)                         # he carries the post
    p.drop("LCB", (19.0, -18.0), speed=4.5)                       # deep third, outside the over
    p.drop("RCB", (17.5, 15.5), speed=4.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=3.1)
    return p


SHOT = shot_play()
animation_or_strip(
    SHOT, times=[0.0, 1.0, 2.4, 4.4],
    notes=["2nd & 1: run look, 8 in the box,\none deep safety (purple)",
           "the fake: linebackers and the\nstrong safety (red) step up",
           "two routes climb behind them;\nthe free safety must pick one",
           "he drifts to the post:\nthe deep over is open"],
    lateral=(-20.5, 20.5), window=(-10.0, 26.0), rings=[("FS", PURPLE), ("SS", RED)])
```

And when teams take the shot, it pays. On second-and-1-to-3 from 2021 to 2025, passes that traveled
15 or more yards in the air averaged `{python} signed(S["deep_epa_2s"])` EPA per attempt, against
`{python} signed(S["run_epa_2s"])` for runs and `{python} signed(S["short_epa_2s"])` for shorter
throws. Yet only about `{python} pct(S["deep_share_2s"])` of second-and-short snaps were a deep throw
(`{python} S["n_deep_2s"]` in five seasons of neutral situations).[^shot] Two cautions belong next to
those numbers. A deep-throw average only counts passes that were thrown, not the sacks taken while
waiting for a deep route to open, so the true value of *calling* the shot is lower. And the shot is a
[constraint play](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-constraint-play): it works because the defense is
leaning toward the run. If every offense threw deep on every second-and-1, defenses would stop
leaning, and the number would shrink. The case the data makes is narrower and still strong: most
offenses could take this shot more often than they do before it stopped paying.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"An incomplete shot on second-and-1 is a wasted down." It's a *spent* down, and it was the cheapest
down the offense will have all game. The offense still has third-and-1, converted more than two times
in three, with fourth-and-1 behind it in much of the field. Compare that with an incompletion on
second-and-10, which leaves third-and-10 and a series that converts about a third of the time.
:::

### The second down after an incompletion

One more second-down habit is worth knowing, because it's a tendency you can see from your couch.
Second-and-10 comes about two ways: after a first-down incompletion, or after a first-down run that
gained nothing. Same down, same distance, so it should be the same call. It isn't. From 2021 to 2025,
offenses threw on `{python} pct(S["pr_after_run"])` of second-and-10s that followed a no-gain run, and
on only `{python} pct(S["pr_after_inc"])` of those that followed an incompletion. The pattern holds a
yard or three shorter, too: on second-and-7-to-9, teams threw `{python} pct(S["pr79_run"])` of the
time after a first-down run and `{python} pct(S["pr79_pass"])` after a first-down pass.[^alt]

Play-callers alternate. After a pass that didn't work, there's a pull toward a run, to avoid two
incompletions in a row and a third-and-10, and to "get back on track" with a sure few yards. After a
run that didn't work, the pull goes the other way. Economists who study play-calling have found the same
habit in NFL data and point out that it's exactly what a perfectly unpredictable caller would *not* do:
in game theory, the right mix of runs and passes shouldn't depend on what you called last
time.[^serial] It's a small edge, but defensive coordinators chart it, and now you can too.

## Field zones: the map on the call sheet

The down and distance tell a play-caller how much freedom he has. The yard line tells him what a
mistake will cost and what success is worth, and the field is not uniform. Coaches divide it into
zones, each with its own box on the call sheet:

```{python}
#| label: fig-field-zones
#| fig-cap: "The field as a play-caller sees it, offense moving left to right. Coaches number yard lines in their own half with a minus sign and in the opponent's half with a plus sign, so 'minus 25' is the offense's own 25 and 'plus 35' the opponent's 35. Backed up runs from the goal line to the minus 10; coming out to about the minus 25; the open field to about the plus 40; four-down territory (the fringe) from there to the plus 20; the red zone inside it. The lines between zones vary by staff and by situation; these are typical. The small triangle marks where a kickoff that lands in the end zone has been spotted since 2025, the minus 35, and the dotted line where field-goal range typically begins for an NFL kicker, around the plus 35."
LAT = (11.0, 42.3)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.7))
Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", los=60, window=None, to_go=None, numbers=False, hashes=False, lateral=LAT)
top, bot = LAT[1], LAT[0]
NAME_AT = {"backed up": 15.0, "coming out": 27.5, "open field": 47.5, "four-down\nterritory": 80.0,
           "red zone": 100.0}
SHOWN = {"backed up": "BACKED\nUP", "coming out": "COMING\nOUT", "open field": "OPEN FIELD",
         "four-down\nterritory": "FOUR-DOWN\nTERRITORY", "red zone": "RED ZONE"}
GOALS = {"backed up": "get out:\nno sack,\nno\nturnover", "coming out": "first first\ndown;\nflip the\nfield",
         "open field": "the whole menu;\nstay on schedule", "four-down\nterritory": "fourth down is\npart of the plan",
         "red zone": "touchdowns,\nnot field goals"}
for name, lo, hi in ZONES:
    x0, x1 = 110 - hi, 110 - lo
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, bot), x1 - x0, top - bot, fc=ZONE_COL[name], alpha=0.16, lw=0, zorder=0.5))
    fs = 6.6 if hi - lo <= 15 else 7.4
    ax.text(NAME_AT[name], (top + bot) / 2 + 5.0, SHOWN[name], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs,
            fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, linespacing=1.0, zorder=6)
    ax.text(NAME_AT[name], (top + bot) / 2 - 5.0, GOALS[name], ha="center", va="center",
            fontsize=5.9 if hi - lo <= 15 else 6.3, color=style.INK_2, linespacing=1.05, zorder=6)
ax.text(80, (top + bot) / 2 + 0.6, "(the fringe)", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2,
        zorder=6)
for x, lab in [(20, MINUS + "10"), (35, MINUS + "25"), (60, "50"), (70, "+40"), (90, "+20")]:
    ax.plot([x, x], [bot, top], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, zorder=3)
    ax.text(x, bot - 1.2, lab, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
for x, t in [(5, "YOUR\nEND ZONE"), (115, "THEIR\nEND ZONE")]:
    ax.text(x, (top + bot) / 2, t, rotation=90, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2)


def bracket(x0, x1, y, text, col=style.INK, fs=7.2):
    ax.plot([x0 + 0.4, x0 + 0.4, x1 - 0.4, x1 - 0.4], [y - 1.6, y, y, y - 1.6], color=col, lw=1.0, clip_on=False)
    ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, y + 1.0, text, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=fs, color=col, clip_on=False)


bracket(10, 60, top + 2.4, "minus territory: your half (" + MINUS + "1 to " + MINUS + "49)")
bracket(60, 110, top + 2.4, "PLUS TERRITORY: their half (+49 to +1)")
ax.plot([75, 75], [bot, top], color=style.INK, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (1, 1.5)), zorder=3)
ax.text(75.7, top - 1.4, "field-goal\nrange begins", ha="left", va="top", fontsize=5.8, color=style.INK_2,
        zorder=6, linespacing=1.0)
ax.plot([45], [bot + 1.8], marker="^", ms=6, color=style.INK, zorder=6)
ax.text(46.4, bot + 2.4, "kickoff\ntouchback", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=5.9, color=style.INK_2, zorder=6,
        linespacing=1.0)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((38.0, top - 2.6), (56.0, top - 2.6), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                             color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.5, zorder=6))
ax.text(47.0, top - 4.4, "offense moving this way", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=5.8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
        zorder=6)
ax.set_ylim(bot - 5.5, top + 7.5)
plt.show()
```

Here is each zone in plain words. The names are the common ones; exact boundaries vary by staff, and
the same staff will move them with the weather, the kicker and the score.[^zones]

- [**Backed up**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-backed-up): inside your own 10. A sack in the end zone,
  or a holding penalty there, is a [safety](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd): two
  points *and* the ball for the other team. Even the punt is cramped, because the punter can't stand at
  his usual depth ([Kicking and Punting](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd)).
- [**Coming out**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coming-out): roughly your own 10 to your own 25. The
  emergency is over, but the offense still wants its first first down, which moves the ball away from
  its goal line and turns a short punt into a long one ("flipping the field").
- [**Open field**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-open-field): roughly your own 25 to the opponent's 40.
  Field position neither forces the offense's hand nor tempts it. Since 2025, a kickoff that lands in the
  end zone comes out to the 35, and about two drives in three now *start* at the offense's own 25 or
  better.[^starts]
- [**Plus territory**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-plus-territory): the opponent's half. Coaches
  write yard lines there with a plus sign ("plus 35") and in their own half with a minus sign ("minus
  25"), so you'll hear a coordinator say "we got the ball in plus territory" after a turnover. The plus
  side isn't one zone; it holds the next two.
- [**Four-down territory**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-down-territory), which coaches also call
  [**the fringe**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fringe): roughly the opponent's 40 to its 20. A punt
  from here buys little field (a little too long and it's a touchback at the 20), and a field goal is
  long or uncertain, so the offense plans on using fourth down if it needs it.
- The [red zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-red-zone), from
  [01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd): inside the opponent's 20, where
  the field compresses and drives cash in or settle for three. It has zones of its own (inside the 10,
  the goal line), which belong to
  [The Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage](10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).

## How the call changes from zone to zone

You can watch the zones change behavior in the data. The top half of the next chart is first-and-10 all
the way down the field; the bottom half is third-and-short.

```{python}
#| label: fig-zone-calls
#| fig-cap: "How the yard line changes the call, neutral situations, 2016-2025 regular seasons, offense moving left to right; each point is a 5-yard stretch of field. Top: on first-and-10 (first-and-goal inside the 10), how often the offense passed (blue) and how often its quarterback lined up in the shotgun (dashed). The pass rate is flat across the open field and falls off at both ends, backed up and near the opponent's goal line; the shotgun disappears when the offense is backed up and, at the other end, only inside the 10. Bottom: on third-and-2-to-4, how often the offense passed. In its own half it threw about seven times in eight; past midfield the rate drops sharply, because fourth down is now part of the plan. Hollow points rest on fewer than 150 snaps. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
def by5(df, col):
    d_ = df.copy()
    d_["b"] = ((d_.yardline_100.clip(1, 99) - 1) // 5) * 5 + 3          # bin centres 3, 8, ..., 98
    t_ = d_.groupby("b")[col].agg(["mean", "size"])
    return 110 - t_.index.values, t_["mean"].values, t_["size"].values


fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.5, 4.4), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.16))
f1 = N10[(N10.down == 1) & ((N10.ydstogo == 10) | (N10.goal_to_go == 1))]
for a in (a1, a2):
    shade_zones(a, alpha=0.08, labels=False)
x_, m_, n_ = by5(f1, "pass")
a1.plot(x_, m_ * 100, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=2, marker="o", ms=3.5, label="pass rate", zorder=3)
x_, m_, n_ = by5(f1, "shotgun")
a1.plot(x_, m_ * 100, color=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="QB in the shotgun", zorder=3)
a1.set_ylim(15, 70)
a1.set_ylabel("1st & 10 (%)", fontsize=8)
a1.legend(loc="lower center", fontsize=7, ncol=2, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0))
for name, lo, hi in ZONES:
    a1.text(110 - (lo + hi) / 2, 68, name.upper().replace("\n", " ") if name != "four-down\nterritory"
            else "FOUR-DOWN TERR.", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=6.0, color=style.INK_2, fontweight="bold")
t3b = N10[(N10.down == 3) & N10.ydstogo.between(2, 4)]
x_, m_, n_ = by5(t3b, "pass")
big = n_ >= 150
a2.plot(x_, m_ * 100, color=style.SERIES[1], lw=2, zorder=3)
a2.scatter(x_[big], m_[big] * 100, s=14, color=style.SERIES[1], zorder=4)
a2.scatter(x_[~big], m_[~big] * 100, s=14, facecolor=style.SURFACE, edgecolor=style.SERIES[1], zorder=4)
a2.axvline(60, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
a2.text(59, 62, "midfield", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
a2.set_ylim(60, 95)
a2.set_ylabel("3rd & 2–4: pass (%)", fontsize=8)
yardline_axis(a2)
for a in (a1, a2):
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

### Backed up: get out, and don't make it worse

Inside its own 10, an offense changes character. On first-and-10 there, teams passed
`{python} pct(S["bu_pr"])` of the time, against `{python} pct(S["of_pr"])` in the open field, and their
quarterbacks were in the shotgun on `{python} pct(S["bu_sg"])` of snaps, against
`{python} pct(S["of_sg"])`. The passes they did call were built not to be sacked: the sack rate on
first-down dropbacks fell from `{python} pct(S["of_sack"], 1)` in the open field to
`{python} pct(S["bu_sack"], 1)` backed up, which means quick throws, play-action with extra blockers, and
quarterbacks told to throw the ball away rather than take the loss.[^backed] The picture shows why the
shotgun in particular goes away.

```{python}
#| label: fig-backed-up
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10 at the offense's own 2 (illustrative). Left: from the shotgun, the quarterback takes the snap five yards behind the ball, three yards deep in his own end zone, and a normal dropback takes him deeper still. Any sack there is a safety, and so is a holding penalty by a blocker in the end zone. Right: under center, with two tight ends, the quarterback takes the snap just in front of his goal line and hands off going forward; even the running back, who lines up in the end zone, gets the ball near the goal line moving out. The call that gets three yards safely is worth more here than the call that might get twenty."
def backed_up_panels():
    LOSb = 12.0      # BDB x of the offense's own 2-yard line
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.55), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.04))
    # A: shotgun dropback
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 7.0, "Y"),
                    O("H", "WR", -1.5, -7.5, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -12.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 12.5, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -1.4, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
           D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 4.8, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -2.5, "W")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOSb, to_go=10)
    for k, w in zip(["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"], (-0.6, -0.2, 0.0, 0.2, 0.6)):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, w)])                     # pass sets
    p.block("RB", pts=[(-0.6, -1.8)])                   # the back stays in to protect
    p.dropback(2.0)
    p.rush("LE", pts=[(-4.0, -2.2), (-7.6, 3.6)])       # edge rushers loop to the quarterback
    p.rush("RE", pts=[(-4.0, 2.0), (-7.6, -3.8)])
    f1 = draw(p, ax=ax1, lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-12.0, 9.0))
    panel_title(ax1, "A. Shotgun at the 2")
    say(f1, p, -10.0, -9.5, "OWN END ZONE", fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
    point_to(f1, p, (-9.2, 8.2), (-7.0, 0.6), "sacked here:\na safety, 2 points\nand the ball",
             color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
    # B: under center, two tight ends, a handoff going forward
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.5, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                    O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"), O("X", "WR", -1.5, -12.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 12.5, "Z")]
    dfn2 = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("LT_", "DT", 1.0, -2.4, "T"), D("RT_", "DT", 1.0, 1.4, "T"),
            D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.2, 1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.2, -2.6, "W"),
            D("SAM", "SAM", 4.2, 5.2, "S")]
    q = Play(off, dfn2, los=LOSb, to_go=10)
    for k in ["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "U", "Y"]:
        q.block(k, pts=[(1.0, 0.3)])
    q.path("QB", [(-0.8, 1.2)], speed=3.0)
    q.run("RB", [(3.6, 1.0), (8.5, 2.0)])
    q.handoff("RB", t=0.75)
    f2 = draw(q, ax=ax2, lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-12.0, 9.0))
    panel_title(ax2, "B. Under center at the 2")
    say(f2, q, -10.0, -9.5, "OWN END ZONE", fontsize=6.6, weight="bold")
    point_to(f2, q, (-9.0, 7.5), (-6.5, 0.0), "even the back\nstarts in the\nend zone", color=style.INK_2)
    say(f2, q, 4.6, -9.5, "3 yards here\nis a good play", fontsize=6.4, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
    return fig


backed_up_panels()
plt.show()
```

Here's the puzzle: by EPA, the run is a *worse* bet backed up than anywhere else on the field (you'll see
it in the EPA chart at the end of the chapter), and the pass still comes out ahead on average, sacks and
safeties included. Why run anyway? Partly the averages again: the backed-up passes that teams do call
are the safe, quick, well-protected kind, chosen precisely because they rarely end in disaster, and a
defense that expected more of them would make them harder. Partly the objective is different. Backed up,
the first goal isn't a big gain, it's *getting out*: a few yards so the punter can stand at his normal
depth, a first down so the next series starts with room. And partly it's the asymmetry Romer described:
a safety or an interception at your own 5 loses a game in a way a three-yard run never does. Backed-up
football is the most conservative football you'll see all day, and for most teams it's also their
least productive: on first-and-10 inside the 10, plays succeeded only `{python} pct(S["bu_sr"])` of the
time, against `{python} pct(S["of_sr"])` in the open field.

### Coming out: the first first down

From its own 10 to about its own 25, an offense's priority is the first first down. Earn it, and the
next punt, if it comes, flips the field from deep in your territory to deep in theirs. Fail, and you
punt from your own 15 and the opponent starts near midfield. You'll see play-callers here lean on
their most reliable first-down calls, the ones they trust not to go backward, but you'll also see the
quarterback come back out in the shotgun and a normal pass rate return: by about the 15 to the 20,
first-and-10 looks like it does everywhere else. Some staffs also keep a box of play-action shots for this zone,
because defenses that just watched a backed-up offense run three times in a row are expecting a fourth.

### The open field: the whole menu

Between the 25s and out to about the opponent's 40, the yard line stops mattering much. First-and-10
pass rates are flat across the whole stretch, and so are shotgun rates. This is where the base plays
live, where [sequencing](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sequencing) does its work and where a
play-caller's balance on first down earns its keep. If you want to learn an offense's personality, watch
it here: the open field is where coaches call what they *like*, not what the field forces on them.

### Plus territory and four-down territory: one more down to spend

Cross midfield and something changes that you can't see on the field: the offense gains a down. Not
officially, but in practice, because once a punt buys little and the kick is long, most offenses now
plan to go for it on fourth-and-short. In 2025 teams went for it on `{python} pct(S["go_plus"])` of
fourth-and-1-to-3s between midfield and the opponent's 21, against `{python} pct(S["go_own"])` in their
own half between their 21 and midfield (outside the last two minutes of each half).[^fourth] That
changes third down. In its own half, an offense facing third-and-2-to-4 threw
`{python} pct(S["t3_own"])` of the time; past midfield, `{python} pct(S["t3_plus"])`. With a fourth down
in hand, third-and-3 becomes the first of two tries, and a run that gains two yards is no longer a
failure: it sets up fourth-and-1. Notice in the bottom panel of the chart where the switch flips:
right at midfield, a little earlier than the "plus 40" that the textbook definition of four-down
territory uses. On short yardage, today's NFL treats the whole plus side as four-down territory.

The defense has to account for this too. On third-and-3 at the opponent's 38, a stop isn't a punt; it's
a fourth-and-short that the offense will probably try. Defensive coordinators call third down
differently when it's the first of two.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Detroit Lions, 2023–2024"}
**The seasons:** Ben Johnson's last two years as Detroit's offensive coordinator under head coach Dan
Campbell. The Lions went 12–5 in 2023 and reached the NFC Championship Game, losing 34–31 in San
Francisco; in 2024 they went 15–2, took the NFC's top seed, and led the league with 564 points before
losing to Washington in the divisional round.[^det]

**What to notice, part 1: balanced and efficient.** On early downs in neutral situations the Lions
passed *less* often than most of the league (`{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2023, "DET"), "pr_rk"])` in 2023,
`{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2024, "DET"), "pr_rk"])` in 2024) and were
`{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2023, "DET"), "epa_rk"])` and `{python} ordinal(TEAM.loc[(2024, "DET"), "epa_rk"])`
in EPA per play. Like the 2018 Rams, they ran and
faked from the same looks, so their run rate was a weapon rather than a price
([Constraint Theory](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd) has their tendency
table).

**What to notice, part 2: they used the extra down.** Campbell's Lions were among the league's most
committed users of four-down territory. They went for it on fourth down
`{python} int(GO.loc[(2023, "DET"), "att"])` times in 2023 (`{python} ordinal(GO.loc[(2023, "DET"), "rk"])` most in
the league) and `{python} int(GO.loc[(2024, "DET"), "att"])` times in 2024
(`{python} ordinal(GO.loc[(2024, "DET"), "rk"])`), converting `{python} int(GO.loc[(2023, "DET"), "conv"])` and
`{python} int(GO.loc[(2024, "DET"), "conv"])`. When an offense will go on fourth down, its *third* down
changes, and so does the defense's: a stop on third-and-3 at the plus 38 isn't a stop yet. The
fourth-down decision itself, and when it pays, is in
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd); the whole
Detroit era is a [case study](../12-case-studies/12-07-lions-ben-johnson-and-campbell.qmd).
:::

### The fringe of field-goal range, and the red zone

Somewhere around the opponent's 35, a drive enters
[field-goal range](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-field-goal-range), and the cost of a negative play
changes again. A sack at the plus 33 doesn't just cost a down and seven yards; it can turn a 51-yard
field goal into a 58-yarder or a punt. That's why you'll see quarterbacks near the edge of range throw
the ball away rather than hold it, and play-callers avoid slow-developing dropbacks on third-and-long
there: three points in hand are worth more than a small chance at a first down.

Inside the 20, the field shrinks. The back of the end zone works like an extra defender, there's no
room to throw over the top, and both pass rates and shotgun rates fall again as the goal line nears.
How offenses and defenses play that compressed field is the next chapter but one,
[The Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage](10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).

## Reading the numbers: down, distance, and yard line

You've now seen the pieces one at a time. Two charts put them together, and they are the kind of chart
you'll meet in every analytics article about play-calling. Here is how to read them.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pass-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "How often offenses passed, by down (rows) and exact yards to go (columns, 15 or more grouped), neutral situations, 2021-2025 regular seasons. Blue cells lean pass, orange cells lean run; grey cells had fewer than 150 snaps. First down is almost always first-and-10; its other cells are mostly first-and-goal inside the 10 and first downs after a penalty. Read across a row to see how fast the pass takes over as the distance grows, and down a column to see what each lost down does at the same distance. Two details are real, not noise: second-and-10 is a *less* pass-heavy cell than second-and-9 (it usually follows an incompletion), and the 1-yard column is run-heavy on every down. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
H = N5[N5.down <= 3].copy()
H["dist"] = H.ydstogo.clip(upper=15).astype(int)
HP = H.pivot_table(index="down", columns="dist", values="pass", aggfunc="mean")
HN = H.pivot_table(index="down", columns="dist", values="pass", aggfunc="size")
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("pr", [style.DEFENSE, "#fbe3d6", "#f6f4ee", style.OFFENSE_TINT,
                                                style.OFFENSE])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.35))
for i, dn in enumerate([1, 2, 3]):
    for j, dist in enumerate(range(1, 16)):
        v, nn = HP.loc[dn, dist], HN.loc[dn, dist]
        rare = nn < 150
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((j, 2 - i), 0.95, 0.92, fc=style.GRID if rare else cmap(float(v)), ec="white", lw=1.2))
        dark = (not rare) and (v >= 0.82 or v <= 0.15)
        ax.text(j + 0.475, 2 - i + 0.46, "·" if rare else f"{v * 100:.0f}", ha="center", va="center",
                fontsize=7.4, fontweight="bold", color="white" if dark else style.INK)
ax.set_xlim(-0.05, 15); ax.set_ylim(-0.05, 3)
ax.set_xticks([j + 0.475 for j in range(15)], [str(k) for k in range(1, 15)] + ["15+"], fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_yticks([2.46, 1.46, 0.46], ["1st down", "2nd down", "3rd down"], fontsize=7.8)
ax.xaxis.tick_top()
ax.xaxis.set_label_position("top")
ax.set_xlabel("Yards to go  (numbers are the % of snaps that were passes)", fontsize=7.6, labelpad=6)
ax.tick_params(length=0); ax.grid(False)
for sp in ax.spines.values():
    sp.set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

A heatmap like this answers "what does the situation *predict*?" It shows the league's habits, not
what's right. Three habits stand out. Across the second-down row, the pass takes over steadily from
about second-and-4. Down the 1-yard column, the run dominates on every down. And across the third-down
row, the switch is nearly instant: by third-and-4 almost everybody throws. Every one of those habits is
a [tendency](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tendency) a defense can lean on, which is why the
interesting calls are the ones that land in the "wrong" color.

```{python}
#| label: fig-epa-field
#| fig-cap: "What runs and dropbacks earned across the field, neutral situations, 2016-2025 regular seasons: EPA per play for designed runs (orange) and dropbacks (blue), by 10-yard stretch of field, offense moving left to right. On first and second down the dropback line sits above the run line almost everywhere; the gap is widest when the offense is backed up and closes near the opponent's goal line, where the field is short and a run is as good as a pass. Third-and-1-to-3 is shown instead of all third downs so that runs and passes face the same distances; it is thinner, so each point there is a whole field zone. Runs have earned about as much as dropbacks or more, and clearly more in the red zone. Points resting on fewer than 150 snaps of either kind are left out, which is why the backed-up end of that panel is empty. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
E = N10.copy()
E["b10"] = ((E.yardline_100.clip(1, 99) - 1) // 10) * 10 + 5
# third-and-short is thinner, so it is binned by field zone (the zone's middle yard line) instead
E["bz"] = E.yardline_100.map(lambda y: next((lo + hi) / 2 for _, lo, hi in ZONES if lo < y <= hi))
panels = [("1st & 10", E[(E.down == 1) & ((E.ydstogo == 10) | (E.goal_to_go == 1))]),
          ("2nd down", E[E.down == 2]), ("3rd & 1–3", E[(E.down == 3) & (E.ydstogo <= 3)])]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 2.8), sharey=True, gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.08))
for a, (title, sub) in zip(axes, panels):
    shade_zones(a, alpha=0.08, labels=False)
    col_ = "bz" if title.startswith("3rd") else "b10"
    t_ = sub.groupby([col_, "pass"]).epa.mean().unstack()
    n_ = sub.groupby([col_, "pass"]).epa.size().unstack()
    t_ = t_.where(n_ >= 150)                    # leave out stretches with too few snaps to trust
    for k, col, lab in [(0, style.SERIES[1], "designed runs"), (1, style.SERIES[0], "dropbacks")]:
        a.plot(110 - t_.index.values, t_[k].values, color=col, lw=1.8, marker="o", ms=3, label=lab, zorder=3)
    a.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
    a.set_title(title, fontsize=8.6)
    a.set_xlim(10, 110)
    a.set_xticks([20, 40, 60, 80, 100], [MINUS + "10", MINUS + "30", "50", "+30", "+10"], fontsize=6.6)
    a.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7)
    a.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[0].set_ylabel("EPA per play", fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_ylim(-0.25, 0.25)
axes[1].legend(loc="lower center", fontsize=7, ncol=2, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.36))
plt.show()
EF = {t: s.groupby(["b10", "pass"]).epa.mean().unstack() for t, s in panels}
```

A chart like this answers a different question: "what did each choice *earn*?" Read it in three steps.
First, find the gap between the lines: on early downs the pass has earned more almost everywhere, by the
most when the offense is backed up, where teams run the most. Second, find where the lines meet: close
to the opponent's goal line, where the defense has no deep space to protect and a run is as good as a
pass. Third, remember what the chart can't see. Every point mixes situations (the backed-up passes are
the safe ones; the third-and-short runs include [quarterback sneaks](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-sneak),
the best short-yardage play in football), and every point is an average of what teams chose to do, not
of what they would have earned doing more of it. The gap is a strong hint about where offenses are too
cautious. It isn't a play-call.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the situation tag"}
This is the [01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) forecaster, upgraded
with the field. For one half of one game, before every snap:

- **Say the tag out loud**: the down-and-distance bucket plus the zone. "Second and short, open field."
  "First and ten, backed up." "Third and three, plus territory."
- **Predict run or pass from the tag**, then glance at the formation and change your guess if it tells
  you something. Mark both.
- **Flag the four situations this chapter gave you an edge in**: second-and-10 after an incompletion
  (lean run); second-and-short with one deep safety and eight defenders near the ball (shot alert: watch
  the safety's eyes); backed up (count the shotgun snaps, and expect a quick throw or a run); third-and-short
  past midfield (expect a run, and a fourth-down try if it fails).
- **At halftime, score yourself by tag**, not just overall. You should be very good on third-and-long and
  second-and-very-long, decent backed up and in the red zone, and close to a coin flip on first-and-10
  and second-and-medium. That isn't a failure: first-and-10 is built to
  beat you.
:::

What "good" looks like: the table below is what you'd score by always guessing the more common call
for each tag, in neutral situations from 2021 to 2025. Overall, that simple rule was right
`{python} pct(S["tag_acc"])` of the time. Beat it on any tag and you're reading something the down and
distance alone don't show.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tags
#| tbl-cap: "The situation tags and how predictable each one was, neutral situations, 2021-2025 regular seasons: the share of snaps that were passes, the more common call, and how often guessing that call would have been right. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
rows = "| Tag | Pass rate | Guess | Right |\n|---|---:|:---:|---:|\n"
for t in TAG_ORDER:
    r_ = TAG_T.loc[t]
    rows += f"| {t} | {pct(r_.pr)} | {r_.guess} | {pct(r_.acc)} |\n"
display(Markdown(rows))
```

## Predict the play

:::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: first-and-10 at your own 3"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-backed-up
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10 at the offense's own 3, second quarter, tied 7-7. The offense has two tight ends (Y and U) and a running back (R) in its own end zone, with the quarterback (Q) under center. The defense has seven men within five yards of the ball and the strong safety (SS) walked down outside the right tight end: eight near the line of scrimmage, one safety (FS) deep."
LOS1 = 13.0
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.5, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                O("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"), O("X", "WR", -1.5, -13.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.5, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("2i", -1), "T"),
       D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E"),
       D("SAM", "SAM", 3.6, 3.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.2, -0.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.2, -3.6, "W"),
       D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 7.8, "SS"), D("LCB", "CB", 5.5, -13.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 5.5, 13.5, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -1.0, "FS")]
p1 = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS1, to_go=10)
f_ = draw(p1, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-12.5, 14.5), width_in=5.6)
say(f_, p1, -9.5, -11.0, "OWN END ZONE", fontsize=7.0, weight="bold")
say(f_, p1, -3.6, 12.5, "goal line", fontsize=6.4)
plt.show()
```

**Run or pass? And name two calls this offense is very unlikely to make.**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Most likely a run, from exactly this kind of look; very unlikely: a shotgun dropback, or any play
that asks the quarterback to hold the ball.**

On first-and-10 inside their own 10, offenses in neutral situations passed only
`{python} pct(S["bu_pr"])` of the time (2016–2025), against `{python} pct(S["of_pr"])` in the open
field. Two tight ends with the quarterback under center make a run more likely still: the quarterback
takes the snap in the field of play and hands off going forward, so the usual worst case for a stuffed run
is second-and-12 at the 1, not a safety.

The calls to cross off are the ones that put the ball behind the goal line for a long time: the
quarterback in the shotgun (he'd start three yards deep in his own end zone), a deep dropback, a pass
that needs four seconds to develop, a stretch run that might be caught going sideways in the end zone.
A sack or a holding penalty in the end zone is two points and the ball.

The surprise you'll occasionally see: a play-action shot from this exact look, with both tight ends and
the back staying in to block, because eight defenders near the line and one deep safety is exactly the
picture a shot is built to beat. It is rare, and when it hits it can go 90-plus yards. The defense knows the odds, which is why it walked the strong safety down: it's betting on the
run, and accepting the risk of the shot.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: second-and-10 after an incompletion"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-2nd-10
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-10 at the offense's own 35, first quarter, tied. On first down the quarterback threw incomplete. The offense is in the shotgun with three receivers and a tight end (11 personnel), the back (R) beside the quarterback. The defense is in its nickel (five defensive backs) with two deep safeties: only six defenders are in the box, inside the tight end and within five yards of the ball."
LOS2 = 45.0
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.0, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("2i", -1), "T"),
       D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("6", 1) + 0.6, "E"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 1.8, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -2.2, "W"), D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.5, "$"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -14.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.5, 8.0, "SS")]
p2 = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS2, to_go=10)
f_ = draw(p2, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-9.5, 15.0), width_in=5.6)
say(f_, p2, -6.2, -11.5, "last play: 1st & 10,\npass incomplete", fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**Run or pass? What does the previous play tell you, and what does the defense tell you?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**More likely a run than the down and distance alone suggest, though a pass is still a slight
favorite.**

Second-and-10 is usually a passing down, but *which* second-and-10 matters. From 2021 to 2025,
offenses threw on `{python} pct(S["pr_after_run"])` of second-and-10s that followed a no-gain run and on
only `{python} pct(S["pr_after_inc"])` of those that followed an incompletion
(`{python} f'{S["n_after_inc"]:,}'` snaps). After a failed pass, play-callers lean toward a run to avoid
two straight incompletions and a third-and-10.

The defense adds a second reason. Two deep safeties and a nickel back leave six defenders in the box
against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end), a [light box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-light-box)
that is all but inviting a run. Many offenses build this answer into the play itself, with a run-pass
option or a quarterback check at the line: against six in the box, hand it off. The defense, for its
part, knows that four or five yards here are not a disaster for it; what it can't allow is the
explosive pass that a single-high shell would risk.

If a pass does come, expect something quick that gets half the distance back: a 5-yard completion turns
the down into third-and-5.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: third-and-3 at the opponent's 38"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-3rd-3
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-3 at the opponent's 38 (plus territory), second quarter, tied. The offense is in the pistol (the quarterback four yards behind the center with the back directly behind him) with three receivers and a tight end. The defense is in its nickel with one deep safety: six defenders in the box, with the nickel back ($) and the strong safety (SS) close enough to fill against a run."
LOS3 = 72.0
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -3.5, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -6.5, 0.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.0, "H"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.5, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("2i", -1), "T"),
       D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, technique("3", 1), "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, technique("6", 1) + 0.8, "E"),
       D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.0, "W"), D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -8.5, "$"),
       D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.5, "SS"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -14.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
p3 = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS3, to_go=3)
f_ = draw(p3, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-9.0, 16.0), width_in=5.6)
plt.show()
```

**Run or pass? Would your answer change if this were third-and-3 at the offense's own 38?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A run is a live option here, much more than it would be in the offense's own half, and if it fails,
expect the offense to stay on the field for fourth down.**

On third-and-2-to-4 from 2016 to 2025, offenses threw `{python} pct(S["t3_own"])` of the time in their
own half and `{python} pct(S["t3_plus"])` of the time past midfield. The yard line is the reason. At the
opponent's 38 a punt buys little and a field goal would be 56 yards, so most offenses plan to use
fourth down: in 2025 teams went for it on `{python} pct(S["go_plus"])` of fourth-and-1-to-3s between
midfield and the opponent's 21. That makes this third down the first of two tries, and a run that gains
two yards isn't a failure; it sets up fourth-and-1.

It also explains why the conversion rate on these third downs barely changes between the two halves of
the field (`{python} pct(S["t3_own_fd"])` in the offense's own half, `{python} pct(S["t3_plus_fd"])`
past midfield): the run isn't a worse call, just a different one. At its own 38, with a punt coming if
it fails, the offense would almost certainly throw, and the defense would know it.

The defense's job changes too. Stopping this play doesn't end the series. A defensive coordinator in
four-down territory has to defend two short-yardage snaps, and the first one can't sell out against the
run or the pass.
:::
::::

## Takeaways

- **The situation comes before the play.** A call sheet is organized by down and distance, field zone,
  and score and clock. On the early downs (first and second) nothing is forced, which is why they are
  where a play-caller's philosophy shows.
- **First-and-10 is a coin flip, on purpose.** Neutral first-down pass rates have sat near 46% for a
  quarter century, even though dropbacks have out-earned runs there every season. Balance keeps the
  defense guessing; the price is the gap. Good offenses shrink the price; they don't abandon balance.
- **"Establish the run" is four claims.** Running doesn't measurably wear defenses down, play-action
  doesn't need a successful run game, and teams run a lot because they're winning, not the reverse. What
  survives: a run game the defense must respect makes the passing game better, and an *efficient* run
  game (2019 Ravens) is worth calling often.
- **Stay on schedule.** About 4 yards on first down is the line between a series that usually converts
  and one that often doesn't. The play that kills drives is the negative play, not the incompletion.
- **Second down comes in four buckets**, and second-and-short is the cheapest down in football to spend
  on a shot: a failed shot costs about half what a wasted second-and-long does. Teams still mostly run
  there, and when they take the shot it usually pays.
- **The field has zones.** Backed up, offenses get conservative and leave the shotgun; in the open field
  the whole menu is available; past midfield, fourth down becomes part of the plan, and third-and-short
  turns into a running down.
